claims.claim: Gender refers to behaviors, personal traits, and social positions that society attributes to being female or male; it is the set of socially constructed roles and expectations attached to sex categories.

Sex refers to physical or physiological differences between females and males, including primary sex characteristics (reproductive system) and secondary characteristics such as height and muscularity; sex and gender are conceptually distinct and the terms are not interchangeable.

Gender socialization occurs through four major agents — family, education, peer groups, and mass media — each of which creates and maintains normative expectations for gender-specific behavior; repeated exposure makes people feel they are acting naturally rather than following a socially constructed role.

Gender roles are the behaviors society expects of women and men; the expectations work like scripts learned through socialization, and society expects people to behave according to their respective gender roles.

Gender stratification is a system in which groups of people experience unequal access to basic, yet highly valuable, social resources along gender lines; in the United States, women earned an average of 85 percent of what men earned in 2024 (median hourly earnings), up from 81 percent in 2003, and women ages 25 to 34 earned 95 cents per dollar earned by men the same age.
The glass ceiling is an invisible barrier that keeps women out of the highest levels of business; in 2021, 41 of the world's largest 500 companies were run by women, about eight percent.

Gender norms vary by time and place: the binary view of gender is specific to certain cultures and is not universal, characteristics of gender vary greatly between societies, and while every society classifies work by gender (a cultural universal, per Murdock's study of 324 societies), the same tasks are not assigned to the same gender everywhere.

Sociologists describe people as doing gender — performing the behaviors attached to their gender in everyday interaction (West and Zimmerman) — and contrast the social-construction view with biological determinism, the belief that men and women behave differently because of biology.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Everyday and legal language often treats 'sex' and 'gender' as synonyms, and some perspectives outside sociology explain behavioral differences between men and women as biologically determined.
positions: OpenStax 12.1 notes that English speakers did not formally distinguish sex from gender until U.S. and British professionals began doing so in the 1950s, and legal usage has shifted since; many people still use the terms interchangeably.

OpenStax 12.2 names biological determinism — the belief that men and women behave differently due to differences in their biology — as the contrasting position to the social-construction view held by sociologists and most social scientists.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: This lesson teaches the mainstream sociological distinction (sex is biological; gender is social) attributed to OpenStax, states the variation of norms factually, and names biological determinism only as the contrast position, without endorsing either side as a policy matter.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Earnings-ratio figures for the gender pay gap vary by data source and year (Pew median hourly earnings vs Census full-time year-round earnings).
positions: Pew Research Center (2025 analysis): women earned 85% of men's median hourly earnings in 2024, 81% in 2003.
U.S. Census Bureau (cited within the Pew analysis): full-time, year-round working women earned 83% of men's earnings in 2023; OpenStax 12.2 cites an older 2017 figure of 80.1%.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson cites the most recent Pew figure (85% for 2024) and attributes it precisely; older figures are not used as current claims.

sourceRecords.title: Introduction to Sociology 3e, 12.1 Sex, Gender, Identity, and Expression
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A per the sociology source-map. Read live 2026-08-22 (openstax.org serves the full server-rendered section HTML). Supports: the working definitions (sex = physical or physiological differences between females and males, including primary sex characteristics such as the reproductive system and secondary characteristics such as height and muscularity; gender = behaviors, personal traits, and social positions that society attributes to being female or male); the statement that sex and gender are not interchangeable; characteristics of gender varying greatly between societies; the binary view of gender as specific to certain cultures and not universal; the 1950s formal distinction of the terms by U.S. and British professionals. Facts synthesized in original wording; no source prose reproduced; lesson examples are original.

sourceRecords.title: Introduction to Sociology 3e, 12.2 Gender and Gender Inequality
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A per the sociology source-map. Read live 2026-08-22 (server-rendered section HTML). Supports: gender roles as scripts learned through socialization; gender socialization through four major agents (family, education, peer groups, and mass media); stratification as a system of unequal access to basic, highly valuable social resources; the glass ceiling (41 of the world's largest 500 companies run by women at the start of 2021, about 8 percent); Murdock's division-of-labor study of 324 societies (all societies classify work by gender — a cultural universal — but the same task is not assigned to the same gender everywhere; men's work given greater prestige in nearly all cases); doing gender (West and Zimmerman: gender is something we do or perform, not something we are); biological determinism as the contrasting view. The section's own 2017/2020 earnings figures were superseded in this lesson by Pew's 2025 analysis. Facts synthesized; no source prose reproduced; lesson examples are original.

sourceRecords.title: Gender pay gap in U.S. has narrowed slightly over 2 decades
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A per the sociology source-map (Pew live). Read live 2026-08-22 by Richard Fry and Carolina Aragão. Supports: in 2024 women earned an average of 85% of what men earned, per a Pew analysis of median hourly earnings of full- and part-time workers; in 2003 women earned 81% as much as men; the wage gap is smaller for workers ages 25 to 34, who earned 95 cents per dollar in 2024; the Census Bureau's most recent analysis shows full-time, year-round working women earned 83% of men's earnings in 2023. Facts synthesized; no excerpts reproduced.
